source.title: Heritage Studies Grade 8: The American Republic, Student Text

learning_objectives.1.1: Explain why the Aztec and Inca empires, for all their size and fighting skill, fell within a few years to small Spanish forces — superior weapons plus epidemic diseases to which the people had no immunity.
learning_objectives.1.2: Explain how environment and food supply shaped the way of life of each of North America's seven Indian regions — permanent villages where food sources were stable, nomadic life where they were not.
learning_objectives.1.3: Distinguish how Spain, France, and England each developed their American claims — Spanish treasure-seeking conquest, French fur-trade outposts under strict royal control, and English colonies of permanent settlers.
learning_objectives.1.4: Explain why England turned to planting American colonies — the defeat of the Spanish Armada (1588) made England the leading sea power, and seven motives, from the chance to own land to religious freedom (the one that set English colonies apart), drove settlers across the Atlantic.
learning_objectives.1.5: Explain why Jamestown nearly failed — gentlemen unwilling to work, a common storehouse that removed the reward for working, disease, and the starving time — and what turned England's first permanent colony around: John Smith's work-or-starve rule, resupply, and tobacco as a cash crop.
learning_objectives.1.6: Explain how technology and trade brought the first Africans to America — Arab and Chinese navigational inventions extended European voyages, the Portuguese joined West Africa's centuries-old trading wealth (Ghana, then Mali, then Songhai), and that trade grew into the transatlantic slave trade that reached Virginia in 1619.
learning_objectives.1.7: Explain how the chapter applies the biblical teaching that all people bear God's image — the achievements of Native American and West African civilizations fulfill the Creation Mandate (Gen. 1:28), while human sacrifice, Columbus's forced conversions, and the Middle Passage violate it.

Chapter 1 → Aztec.text: The Aztec empire began in the AD 1200s in Mexico and was built around war. Its people drained swampland to raise Tenochtitlan, the huge city where Mexico City now stands, and watered their crops with advanced irrigation. Montezuma was still adding territory when Spanish conquistadors — conquerors — brought the empire down. Fighting, plus diseases the people had no defense against, cut their population roughly in half between 1519 and 1521. Spanish weapons, not Aztec numbers, decided it.

Chapter 1 → Olmec and Maya.text: The Olmec farmed southern Mexico centuries before Christ and carved giant stone heads; their influence faded by about 400 BC. The Maya reached the rainforests of southern Mexico and Guatemala before 1000 BC and entered a golden age about AD 250, building cities with temples and step pyramids. Both wrote in symbols resembling Egypt's hieroglyphics, both studied the sky, and both worked out a 365-day calendar. The Maya worshiped many gods and practiced human sacrifice.

Chapter 1 → Inca.text: The Incan empire ran in a long, narrow strip down the western side of South America, at about the same time as the Aztec empire. Its builders raised remarkable works in hard-to-reach places, such as the mountaintop city of Machu Picchu, and linked many cities by roads. Ten years after the Aztecs fell, conquistadors came: Francisco Pizarro wanted the famous Incan gold, kidnapped and later executed the ruler, and beat Incan resistance with better weapons. Smallpox killed millions.

Chapter 1 → Early American Civilizations.text: How the first people reached the Americas is uncertain. The chapter starts from Genesis 11: after languages were confused at Babel, people scattered over the earth, and some may have crossed a land bridge from Asia to Alaska or come by water. However they arrived, they were living here long before Europeans. They divided into hundreds of tribes, each with its own language, way of life, and chief — some nomadic, moving after game and wild plants, others settled farmers.

Chapter 1 → Native American Culture and.text: Europeans often called native peoples backward or savage, missing the abilities God gives every image-bearer. In fact they shaped their world skillfully — ruins in Central America, cliff houses and irrigation in the Southwest, eastern forests burned clear to make hunting easier — unknowingly obeying God's charge to "fill" and "subdue" the earth. Some also misused it, overhunting or burning useful trees. Most northern religion rested on the Great Spirit and on animism: everything, living or not, has a soul.

Chapter 1 → Northwest Coast.text: Villages here stood along the ocean and the rivers running into it, and the water fed them well: salmon from the streams, oysters and fish from the sea. Cedar supplied sturdy houses, and the tallest trees were carved into totem poles that recorded a family's history, local legends, and important events.

Chapter 1 → Great Basin and Plateau.text: Between the Rockies and the western coastal mountains lived the Shoshone, Ute, Nez Perce, and others — hunter-gatherers who kept moving. The climate was harsh and the land would not farm, so they lived on wild nuts and berries, small game, and fish. They wove baskets and left petroglyphs, rock drawings that picture their way of life. Many later took up tepees and bison hunting like the Plains tribes.

Chapter 1 → Southwest.text: Across today's Southwest — Colorado, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico — skilled builders and masons cut elaborate houses into cliff faces, laid out many-roomed homes resembling apartments, and mixed clay with straw to make adobe. Navajo families often built hogans of logs and earth. Food in this dry country came three ways for the Pueblo, Apache, Hopi, and Navajo: crops raised in the desert, plants collected wild, and small animals hunted. The region's turquoise jewelry, pottery, and weaving are famous.

Chapter 1 → Arctic and Subarctic.text: Near the Arctic Circle — in what are now Canada, Alaska, and Greenland — the Inuit built their whole way of life out of whatever that frozen country offered. Blocks of snow and ice became igloos. Caribou, whales, seals, and walruses supplied food and clothing; whale oil burned for light; and skins from hunted animals covered small boats and kayaks.

Chapter 1 → Eastern Woodlands.text: Woodland tribes lived in the East, from the Atlantic to the Mississippi. The Algonquian, Huron, and others hunted and fished but also planted maize, squash, and tobacco; because that food supply held steady, their villages were permanent. Many homes were wigwams — dome-shaped, covered with leaves, bark, or skins — while the Iroquois built long rectangular houses for extended families. The Iroquois later formed an alliance called the League of Five Nations.

Chapter 1 → Southeast.text: In the Ohio Valley and the Southeast, people raised mounds of earth used as tombs or for religious ceremonies. Ohio's Great Serpent Mound is the one the chapter singles out. The greatest cluster stood at Cahokia, where Missouri and Illinois meet; in 1200 it was the largest pre-Columbian city in North America, holding more people than London did that year. Cherokee, Seminole, and Creek tribes also lived in the region.

Chapter 1 → Great Plains.text: On the prairies between the Mississippi and the Rockies, tribes often settled in small villages beside rivers and lakes. Once horses reached them they moved far more, roaming the grasslands after bison and living in tepees, which were easy to transport. The Sioux, Cheyenne, and Blackfoot grew powerful there. These are the tribes that older cowboy movies usually pictured.

Chapter 1 → The Spanish.text: Before the 1400s ships could not handle rough water far from land, so few Europeans sailed out of sight of shore. The Portuguese fixed that by fitting small fishing boats with specially designed sails; the fast ships that resulted were called caravels. New instruments helped with navigation too. Merchants and monarchs paid for voyages because the Indies promised spices, silk, porcelain, gems, and precious metals — and some believed the East could be reached by sailing west.

Chapter 1 → Columbus's Search for the In.text: Columbus, an Italian sailor, could not persuade Portugal to fund him, so Spain's Ferdinand and Isabella did. He sailed in August 1492 with three ships and sighted land on October 12, calling the people Indians because he thought he had reached the East Indies. He hoped to spread Catholicism but went about it wrongly, mistreating the people and carrying some to Spain as slaves. Vespucci later argued the coasts were a new world; a German mapmaker named it for him.

Chapter 1 → Other Spanish Explorers.text: Spain explored the Central and South American coasts first, then pushed inland behind the conquistadors. Because the treasure lay south, most of Spain's attention stayed there, though a few conquistadors hunted wealth farther north and won Spain claims in Florida, Texas, and the Southwest. Spain planted its language, customs, and Roman Catholic faith wherever it claimed land. It carried corn and potatoes home and brought horses and cattle over. Warfare, slavery, and epidemics devastated the natives.

Chapter 1 → The French.text: France looked for a northern water route to the Far East and, through the 1600s, settled along the St. Lawrence and Mississippi and around the Great Lakes. Lakes and rivers worked like roads into the interior, where trading tools and clothing for beaver, fox, otter, and moose skins paid well. Instead of organized towns the French built forts, missions, and trading posts. Few settlers came: little quick wealth, no self-rule under a controlling king, and after the mid-1600s no Protestants.

Chapter 1 → Sea Dogs and the Spanish Arm.text: English captains called Sea Dogs raided Spanish ports and captured treasure ships, which infuriated Spain; the most famous, Sir Francis Drake, was knighted by Elizabeth I aboard the Golden Hind. Religion sharpened the quarrel, since England had turned Protestant and Philip II wanted it Catholic again. In 1588 his 130-ship Armada met faster English ships in the Channel, was badly beaten, and lost more vessels to storms. England replaced Spain at sea, opening the way to colonize.

Chapter 1 → Reasons for Colonization.text: The chapter gives seven motives for English colonies. Land came first for ordinary people, since wealthy families held nearly all of England's. Then political freedom, as kings clawed back rights the Magna Carta had guaranteed; personal riches for colonists and their investors; adventure in a barely known world; English domination, to check Spain and Catholicism; national wealth from raw materials and new markets; and religious freedom — the motive that set English colonies apart.

Chapter 1 → The Lost Colony.text: Sir Walter Raleigh never sailed to America but paid for two colonies on Roanoke Island. The 1585 attempt broke down under famine, Indian attacks, and poor leadership, and the settlers went home a year later. In 1587 John White led a second group, then returned to England for supplies; war with Spain delayed him three years. He found the colony empty — his granddaughter Virginia Dare gone with the rest, and only the word Croatoan cut in a tree.

Chapter 1 → Jamestown.text: In May 1607 the Virginia Company sent over a hundred men and boys to Chesapeake Bay, where they built Jamestown on the James River. Gentlemen who thought work beneath them hunted gold, and men who did plant crops quit once the whole harvest went into one common storehouse. Bad water and mosquitoes brought disease. John Smith's rule — no work, no food — revived the colony until injury sent him home, and the starving time of 1609-10 left sixty alive.

Chapter 1 → Empires in Western Africa.text: For centuries the West African empires had grown enormously rich on trade in gold, ivory, salt, and slaves. Ghana, far north of today's country of that name, built a trading post at the Sahara's edge and taxed everything entering and leaving; its height came about AD 1000, and it faded once gold was found elsewhere. Mali absorbed it, took Timbuktu and Gao, and grew famous through Mansa Musa's wealth. Songhai, ruling from Gao, then broke free and replaced Mali.

Chapter 1 → Middle Eastern Contributions.text: Arab scholars put their knowledge of the stars and their advanced mathematics to work designing tools for sea travel. The astrolabe, which they improved, lined the horizon up with star coordinates to give a ship its direction and the time — priceless to anyone sailing toward unknown lands. The sextant, also an Arab invention, eventually replaced it. Both were the cutting-edge technology of their day, and both kept providing evidence that the world is round.

Chapter 1 → Chinese Contributions.text: China worked out many mathematical and scientific ideas of its own. Its sailors used magnetic and later floating compasses, and its careful records of the stars produced accurate star charts for use on clear nights. Combined with knowledge from Islamic advisers, this opened a Chinese age of sea exploration whose high point was Zheng He's seven voyages during the Ming dynasty; he reached India, Arabia, and much of East Africa, bringing giraffes home for the emperor.

Chapter 1 → Africans in America.text: In 1619, the year the first large group of women reached Jamestown, a Dutch ship landed about twenty Africans in Virginia. The evidence points to their being held as indentured servants: people who worked a set number of years to repay an Atlantic crossing, and went free afterward. Soon, though, nearly every African brought over came as a slave: about five times the cost of a servant, held for life, with any children counted as the master's property.

Chapter 1 → Esteban.text: Esteban, a Moroccan slave belonging to a Spanish explorer, joined a party exploring Cuba and Florida in the early 1500s. Chased by natives, the group wrecked near Galveston; of eighty survivors held captive, only four escaped, and they wandered the Southwest for years before reaching Spanish forces. Sold to the governor of Mexico City, he scouted ahead of a friar toward the fabled cities of Cibola, sending back crosses sized to the wealth he found — until natives killed him.

Chapter 1 → The Middle Passage.text: The Middle Passage was the Atlantic crossing that carried captured Africans to the Americas — the second leg, after the march to the African coast and before the final sale. Traders packed the ships to make the most money, so people lay stacked or chained side by side for five weeks to four months, in filth and foul air. Disease spread fast, and the sick were sometimes thrown overboard. Food was rice, cornmeal, or yams twice a day.

items.stem: The chapter calls the Spanish soldiers who overthrew the Aztec empire conquistadors. What does that word mean?
options: Missionaries — Spanish priests sent out to teach the Indians Catholicism
Mapmakers — Spanish sailors who charted the coastlines of the Americas
Conquerors — Spanish soldiers who seized native empires by force
Merchants — Spanish traders who exchanged goods with the native peoples

items.stem: The chapter says one group of early American peoples wrote with symbols much like the hieroglyphics of ancient Egypt. Which group was it?
options: The Iroquois and the Huron
The Olmec and the Maya
The empires of Ghana and Mali
The Aztec and the Inca

items.stem: The Aztecs had a huge population and were skilled fighters, yet a much smaller Spanish force brought their empire down. How does the chapter explain that?
options: Neighboring tribes joined the Spanish, and Montezuma handed over his capital city without any fight at all
Spanish ships blockaded the coast, and a long famine emptied the storehouses of the capital, Tenochtitlan
The Aztecs had already left their cities behind, so the Spanish walked into a capital that stood empty
Spanish weapons were better, and diseases the Aztecs could not fight off cut their numbers about in half

items.stem: True or false: According to the chapter, the Aztec empire was still expanding when the Spanish overthrew it.
options: True
False
justify_options: The chapter says Montezuma was still adding territory when the conquistadors overthrew the empire
The chapter says the Aztecs had just finished conquering the Maya cities to their south and to the east
The chapter says the Aztecs were still draining new swampland to make Tenochtitlan even larger

items.stem: How does the chapter explain the fall of the Incan empire?
options: The Inca and the Aztec wore each other down in a long war, and the Spanish simply took what was left over
The Inca abandoned their mountain cities and let their roads crumble, so the Spanish found almost nobody there
The Inca handed over their gold to buy peace, and the Spanish went home and left the empire to its own rulers
Pizarro seized and executed its ruler, Spanish weapons again proved stronger, and smallpox killed millions

items.stem: The chapter calls some of the first American peoples nomadic. What does that mean?
options: They stayed in one village and farmed the same fields year after year
They followed a single chief who ruled over many tribes at the same time
They kept moving from place to place to find game and wild plants
They traveled far to trade, but always returned to the same home town

items.stem: The chapter defines animism. What is it?
options: The belief that the sun grows weak unless people offer it sacrifices
The belief that every natural object, living or not, has a soul
The belief that a chief becomes a god after he dies bravely in battle
The belief that one Great Spirit made the world and then left it alone
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Native American Culture and Religion

items.stem: Before the 1400s few Europeans sailed far from shore, because their ships could not handle rough water. What does the chapter say changed that?
options: The Dutch designed wide cargo ships that could hold far more men and more supplies
The Portuguese fitted small fishing boats with special sails, making fast ships called caravels
The Spanish began building heavy warships that could carry rows of cannon safely across the open ocean
The Vikings taught European shipwrights how to build longships out of northern pine

items.stem: How did America get its name, according to the chapter?
options: An Italian merchant named it after the port his own ships had sailed from
Sailors named it for the Indians that Columbus met on the first islands
Columbus named the new land for the Spanish queen who paid his way
A German mapmaker named the continent for Amerigo Vespucci
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Columbus's Search for the Indies

items.stem: How did Spain develop its claims in the Americas, according to the chapter?
options: Traders set up posts along the lakes and rivers and swapped tools, pots, and cloth for beaver and fox skins
Conquistadors pushed inland hunting treasure, and Spain planted its language, customs, and Catholic faith
Sailors mapped the coastline and went home again, leaving the land empty for settlers who came later
Families crossed over to farm land of their own and to worship the way they believed was right

items.stem: True or false: According to the chapter, France's colonies in North America attracted large numbers of settlers.
options: True
False
justify_options: There was little quick wealth, the king allowed no self-rule, and after the mid-1600s only Roman Catholics could settle
The northern land was far too cold for any crops to grow, so the families who tried to settle could not feed themselves there
The Huguenots filled the French colonies up so quickly that there was no land left for any of the newcomers who kept arriving

items.stem: The chapter sums up what the three main European countries were doing in the Americas. Which summary matches it?
options: Spain built farming towns, France hunted whales, and England kept searching for a sea route to the Indies
Spain traded furs, France mined silver, and England sent its navy to guard the coastline for the king
Spain mined riches, France ran the fur trade, and England took another path with lasting settlements
Spain claimed the far north, France claimed Florida, and England claimed the islands of the Caribbean

items.stem: Who were the Sea Dogs?
options: Dutch traders who carried English goods to markets all around the Caribbean
Spanish captains who guarded the treasure fleets sailing home from the Americas
English sea captains who raided Spanish ports and seized treasure ships
English merchants who paid for the first colonies planted on Roanoke Island
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Sea Dogs and the Spanish Armada

items.stem: One Sea Dog sailed all the way around the world plundering Spanish ports. The Spanish called him the 'master thief,' but Queen Elizabeth I knighted him on the deck of his ship, the Golden Hind. Who was he?
options: Sir Francis Drake
John Cabot
Lord De La Warr
Sir Walter Raleigh
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Sea Dogs and the Spanish Armada

items.stem: Why does the chapter say the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588 mattered so much for America?
options: Spain gave up its colonies in Mexico and Peru, and English settlers moved into them within a few years
England captured the whole Spanish treasure fleet, and that gold paid for the first English settlements
The Sea Dogs stopped their raids, and Spain and England agreed to divide North America between them
Spain never recovered, England became the leading sea power, and the way opened for English colonies
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Sea Dogs and the Spanish Armada

items.stem: Who sent the colonists who founded Jamestown in 1607?
options: The Virginia Company, a group of London merchants
The Church of England, which wanted a mission to the Indians
The royal navy, under direct orders from King James I
Sir Walter Raleigh, who had already tried twice at Roanoke

items.stem: When John White finally returned to Roanoke Island after three years away, what was the only clue he found?
options: The word Croatoan carved into a tree
A church bell buried deep under the sand
A row of fresh graves beside the fort's wall
A letter left behind inside an empty house

items.stem: The Jamestown men who did plant crops stopped working. Why, according to the chapter?
options: John Smith sent every able man off to search the riverbanks for gold instead of putting in a crop of food
Everything they harvested went into a common storehouse for everyone, so working brought them nothing more
The Powhatan Indians kept carrying off the harvest, so the colonists saw no point in planting any more of it
Malaria from the swamps left so many of them too sick to stand up long enough to work out in the fields

items.stem: What did John Smith do that helped Jamestown survive?
options: He sailed home for supplies and came back with a new governor and a hundred more settlers
He moved the entire settlement upriver to dry ground that was free of the swamp mosquitoes
He ruled that a man who would not work would not eat, and he worked right beside them
He broke up the common storehouse into private plots and gave every man a share of his own

items.stem: Put these events in the order the chapter tells them.
options: The 'starving time' of the winter of 1609-10 leaves only about sixty of the colonists alive
Gentlemen refuse to work, the men who farm give up on the common storehouse, and food runs short
Three ships from the Virginia Company reach Chesapeake Bay, and the colonists build Jamestown
The House of Burgesses meets and begins passing laws for the good of the colony
John Smith rules that a man who will not work will not eat, and the settlement goes back to work

items.stem: Why does the chapter say the Virginia House of Burgesses mattered?
options: It was the first representative assembly in America, where burgesses passed laws for the colony
It was the first royal court in America, where the king's judges settled quarrels among settlers
It was the first church council in America, where ministers set the rules for colonial worship
It was the first trading company in America, where merchants fixed the price of the tobacco crop

items.stem: What did the astrolabe do for explorers, according to the chapter?
options: It kept a ship's drinking water fresh even on the very longest ocean voyages
It told direction and time by lining up the horizon with the stars
It drew a map of the coastline as the ship sailed along past it
It measured how deep the water was beneath a ship's wooden hull

items.stem: The chapter tells the story of an African who wandered the Southwest with Spanish explorers in the early 1500s, a hundred years before Africans landed at Jamestown. Who was he?
options: Mansa Musa, the wealthiest ruler of the empire of Mali
Amerigo Vespucci, the merchant the new continent was named for
Zheng He, the Chinese admiral of seven long sea voyages
Esteban, a Moroccan slave of a Spanish explorer

items.stem: Put the three great trading empires of West Africa in the order the chapter says they rose.
options: Mali, which absorbed Ghana and became famous through the wealth of Mansa Musa
Songhai, whose rulers at Gao broke away and then took Mali's place
Ghana, which grew rich taxing the goods that crossed the edge of the Sahara

items.stem: How did the empire of Ghana become so rich?
options: It sat at the edge of the Sahara and taxed the goods coming into and going out of the empire
It seized the gold mines of Mali and made their owners hand over half of everything they dug up
It sold its salt to Portugal in exchange for horses, weapons, and ships built for ocean voyages
It charged every pilgrim a fee to cross its territory on the long road toward the city of Mecca

items.stem: What does the chapter say China contributed to the age of exploration?
options: Magnetic and floating compasses, plus careful star charts that could be used on clear nights
The astrolabe and the sextant, tools that lined the horizon up with the coordinates of the stars
The caravel, a small fast ship whose sails were designed for long voyages far out at sea
Printed maps of the Atlantic that showed the islands lying to the west of the African coast

items.stem: What does the chapter say about the roughly twenty Africans a Dutch ship brought to Virginia in 1619?
options: They were carried straight on to the Caribbean, so none of them stayed in Virginia for any length of time
They appear to have been treated as indentured servants, though soon nearly all Africans came as slaves
They were free men hired to work in the tobacco fields for the wages the planters had agreed to pay
They were sold at once as slaves, and after them no African ever reached the colonies as anything else

items.stem: The chapter begins its account of how people reached the Americas with an event from the Bible. Which one?
options: The call of Abraham, after which he and his family journeyed to a new land
The confusing of languages at the tower of Babel, after which people scattered
The exodus from Egypt, after which Israel wandered forty years in the wilderness
The flood of Noah, after which the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat

items.stem: What was the 'Middle Passage'?
options: The narrow channel where the English navy met the ships of the Spanish Armada
The water route the French kept hoping to find through North America
The ocean crossing that carried captured Africans to the Americas
The overland road that carried salt south across the Sahara desert

items.stem: The chapter says Native Americans were fulfilling the Creation Mandate of Genesis 1:28 without knowing it. What does it point to?
options: The way they gathered into cities and chose one chief to rule all the tribes of a region
The way they shaped the land — cliff houses, irrigation, forests burned clear for hunting
The way they kept their history in writing so that later people could read what they did
The way they set aside land where nobody hunted, so that the animals would never run short
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Native American Culture and Religion

items.stem: The chapter says Columbus hoped to spread Catholicism but 'tried to spread his religion the wrong way.' What does it mean by that?
options: He mistreated the Indians and took some to Spain as slaves, forcing his faith on them
He refused to let any priests sail with him, so nobody aboard could teach the Indians the faith
He gave the islands religious names but never explained to the Indians what those names meant
He let the Indians go on worshiping their own gods rather than telling them about the true God
items.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Columbus's Search for the Indies

items.stem: True or false: According to the chapter, the same English colonists who wanted freedom for themselves did not always give that freedom to others.
options: True
False
justify_options: Africans were soon brought as slaves who worked for a master all their lives, and their children became his property too
Colonists kept indentured servants at work for the rest of their lives instead of freeing them when their agreed years were finished
Colonists required the Powhatan Indians to attend the Church of England and to pay the taxes that supported it

shared_options.theme: getting property of your own, which was nearly impossible in England
shared_options.correction: the reason the chapter calls most important for common people — wealthy families held nearly all English land and tradition kept them from selling it, so a man who inherited none had little hope of ever owning any

shared_options.theme: escaping kings who were taking back rights that had been guaranteed
shared_options.correction: the second motive — the Magna Carta of 1215 limited the monarch and guaranteed basic rights, but kings in the 1600s tried to strengthen royal power, and many Englishmen left to get away from that rule

shared_options.theme: profit for the colonist, or for the investor who paid his way over
shared_options.correction: the third motive — investors paid the expenses of many colonists, hoping that raw materials sent back from the colonies would return them a healthy profit

shared_options.theme: excitement, because so little was known about the new lands
shared_options.correction: the fourth motive — a new world inspired dreams of adventure, though the chapter adds that the reality of hardship often ruined the excitement

shared_options.theme: blocking Spain and stopping the spread of Catholicism
shared_options.correction: the fifth motive — England wanted to stop the advance of Spain, and the king, as head of the Church of England, hoped that converting the Indians would keep them from allying with the Spanish

shared_options.theme: what the whole country gains: raw materials and new markets for its goods
shared_options.correction: the sixth motive — permanent colonies would supply raw materials and create new markets for England's goods, trade by which England hoped to compete with Spain's great wealth

shared_options.theme: escaping a country where the law required one church of everybody
shared_options.correction: the seventh motive, and the one the chapter says set English colonies apart from other European colonies — everyone in England had to attend and pay taxes for the Church of England, and some who disagreed were severely punished

questions.focus: owning property, which almost no ordinary Englishman could hope to do at home
questions.stem: Thomas rents the fields he farms. Nearly all the ground around him belongs to a few wealthy families who will not sell it, and he has no relative who will leave him any. Then he hears sailors praising how much open country there is in America. Which of the seven reasons for colonizing is this?

questions.focus: getting out from under a king who was taking back rights already guaranteed
questions.stem: A group of Englishmen complain that the king is clawing back rights their grandfathers were promised when the Magna Carta limited what a monarch could do. Rather than live under a stronger royal hand, they decide to leave for America. Which of the seven reasons for colonizing is this?

questions.focus: the private profit expected by the men who paid the bill
questions.stem: A group of London businessmen never plan to sail anywhere themselves. They pay the costs for a shipload of colonists, expecting that the timber and other raw materials sent home will earn them a solid return. Which of the seven reasons for colonizing is this?

questions.focus: the pull of the unknown, before any hardship has been felt
questions.stem: Two young men know almost nothing about the new lands, and that is exactly why they want to go. They picture a voyage full of excitement. The chapter warns that men like them found more hardship than they had bargained for. Which of the seven reasons for colonizing is this?

questions.focus: stopping a rival country and its church, not enriching anybody
questions.stem: The English king, who is head of the Church of England, wants Spain's advance halted. He hopes that Indians who are converted will not make alliances with the Spanish. Which of the seven reasons for colonizing is this?

questions.focus: what the whole nation gains from trade, not what one settler or investor gains
questions.stem: Advisers tell the king that permanent colonies would send home raw materials and would also buy English goods, and that this trade could help England match Spain's riches. Which of the seven reasons for colonizing is this?

questions.focus: escaping a country where the law required everyone to belong to one church
questions.stem: A family disagrees with some of the practices of the one church every Englishman must attend and pay taxes to support. Friends of theirs have been punished for their beliefs. They sail for America hoping to worship as they believe God's Word teaches. Which of the seven reasons for colonizing is this?

bank_meta.status: UNVETTED — draft. A SECOND Chapter 1 bank, additional to the primary bank (set_id ""), scoped to the class teacher's 38-card Quizlet study set: the Quizlet supplies the SCOPE, the chapter supplies the TRUTH. Every card is covered by at least one item, and deliberate redundancy tests the same fact from more than one angle. Where a card and the chapter disagree, the chapter governs and the item is keyed to it — de Soto's start is 1539 (card says 1540s); the mound builders are placed in the Ohio Valley AND the Southeast (card names only the Southeast); tobacco is a profitable cash crop, not the thing that saved the colony (the chapter credits resupply, De La Warr, and food crops as well); Tenochtitlan is the large city the Aztecs built on drained swampland, which the chapter never calls their capital; Esteban is 'considered' the first African in America; the explorer is Champlain, not 'Chaplain'; and the chapter attributes the mathematics-and-astronomy achievements to the Olmec and Maya rather than to Native Americans generally. No Tier-3 items and no scenario_mc: Chapter 1 has no Tier-3 candidate, so no cover test applies. No item is built on the chapter's known factual errors (errata §3): the sugar Fun Fact, the Maya Long Count '2012', Pizarro's kinship to Cortés, the Great Serpent Mound 'largest in the world', and the totem-pole claim. Grade-8 audience. Instructor review required before release.

source.title: Heritage Studies Grade 8: The American Republic, Student Text

learning_objectives.1.1: Explain why the Aztec and Inca empires, for all their size and fighting skill, fell within a few years to small Spanish forces — superior weapons plus epidemic diseases to which the people had no immunity.
learning_objectives.1.2: Explain how environment and food supply shaped the way of life of each of North America's seven Indian regions — permanent villages where food sources were stable, nomadic life where they were not.
learning_objectives.1.3: Distinguish how Spain, France, and England each developed their American claims — Spanish treasure-seeking conquest, French fur-trade outposts under strict royal control, and English colonies of permanent settlers.
learning_objectives.1.4: Explain why England turned to planting American colonies — the defeat of the Spanish Armada (1588) made England the leading sea power, and seven motives, from the chance to own land to religious freedom (the one that set English colonies apart), drove settlers across the Atlantic.
learning_objectives.1.5: Explain why Jamestown nearly failed — gentlemen unwilling to work, a common storehouse that removed the reward for working, disease, and the starving time — and what turned England's first permanent colony around: John Smith's work-or-starve rule, resupply, and tobacco as a cash crop.
learning_objectives.1.6: Explain how technology and trade brought the first Africans to America — Arab and Chinese navigational inventions extended European voyages, the Portuguese joined West Africa's centuries-old trading wealth (Ghana, then Mali, then Songhai), and that trade grew into the transatlantic slave trade that reached Virginia in 1619.
learning_objectives.1.7: Explain how the chapter applies the biblical teaching that all people bear God's image — the achievements of Native American and West African civilizations fulfill the Creation Mandate (Gen. 1:28), while human sacrifice, Columbus's forced conversions, and the Middle Passage violate it.

Chapter 1 → Early American Civilizations.text: Genesis 11 is where the chapter begins: languages were confused at Babel and people spread over the earth. Route and date are both uncertain — a land bridge joining Asia to Alaska is one possibility, arrival by water another — but these peoples were here long before any European. Hundreds of separate tribes formed, each with its own chief, language, and way of life. Nomadic ones kept moving after game and wild plants; others settled and raised crops.

Chapter 1 → Olmec and Maya.text: Olmec means rubber people, a name earned by the uses this people found for the rubber tree. They grew maize and cassava in southern Mexico centuries before Christ, cut colossal heads from basalt, and had faded by roughly 400 BC. The Maya settled the rainforests of southern Mexico and modern Guatemala, and about AD 250 their cities, temples, and step pyramids entered a golden age. Sky-watching plus mathematics yielded a 365-day calendar for both peoples.

Chapter 1 → Aztec.text: Later than the Olmec and the Maya, an Aztec warrior empire took shape in Mexico during the AD 1200s. Swampland was drained to make room for Tenochtitlan — modern Mexico City sits on that spot — and irrigation carried water to the fields. Montezuma ruled a state still growing when Spain's conquistadors, whose name means conquerors, ended it. Between 1519 and 1521 warfare and unfamiliar disease cut the people to about half. Skill and numbers lost to better weapons.

Chapter 1 → Southwest.text: Cliff dwellers is the chapter's name for the Southwestern tribes who carved elaborate houses into cliff faces across present-day Colorado, Utah, Arizona, and New Mexico. Expert architects and masons, they also laid out apartment-like homes of many rooms and used adobe, a clay-and-straw mixture dried hard. Navajo families often preferred hogans of logs and earth. Pueblo, Apache, Hopi, and Navajo households drew food three ways: crops raised in dry ground, wild plants collected, and small animals hunted.

Chapter 1 → Southeast.text: Two areas — the Ohio Valley and the Southeast — were home to the mound builders, whose mounds of earth served as tombs or as sites for religious ceremonies. The mounds clustered most thickly at Cahokia, on the ground where Missouri and Illinois now meet; that city held more people in 1200 than London did. The Cherokee, the Seminole, and the Creek were among the tribes living in this region.

Chapter 1 → Arctic and Subarctic.text: Everything the Inuit needed came out of the frozen country they settled around the Arctic Circle, in present-day Canada, Alaska, and Greenland. Snow and ice, cut into blocks, made igloos. Hunting supplied the rest: caribou, whales, seals, and walruses for food and clothing, whale oil to burn for light, and hides to stretch over kayaks and other small boats.

Chapter 1 → Eastern Woodlands.text: Steady food explains the permanent villages of the Eastern Woodlands. Tribes such as the Algonquian and the Huron hunted and fished, but they also planted maize, squash, and tobacco, so there was no need to move on. Their country ran from the Atlantic west to the Mississippi. Wigwams — round-topped shelters covered in bark, leaves, or skins — were common, while Iroquois families shared long rectangular houses. An Iroquois alliance, the League of Five Nations, came later.

Chapter 1 → Native American Culture and.text: Calling the native peoples backward or savage, as Europeans often did, overlooked what God grants everyone who bears His image. Evidence of that gift fills the chapter: Central American ruins, Southwestern cliff houses and irrigation, Atlantic forests burned to ease hunting and travel. Such work fulfilled God's charge to "fill" and "subdue" the earth without the builders knowing it. In the north, belief in the Great Spirit led on to animism: souls in every natural object, living or not.

Chapter 1 → The Vikings.text: Evidence in eastern Canada shows that Vikings — Norse seamen out of northern Europe — reached North America about AD 1000. Colonies in Iceland and Greenland came first, and from Greenland they sailed west to Canada. The best known of them, Leif Ericson, found land in present-day Newfoundland and named it Vinland. Other Norsemen probably followed him, but the rest of Europe never learned of any of those voyages.

Chapter 1 → The Spanish.text: Fishing boats rebuilt with specially designed sails gave Portugal the caravel, a fast ship able to take the open sea; before the 1400s, rough water away from shore had kept most European sailors close to home. Better navigating instruments arrived as well. What made a voyage worth financing was the Indies — the chapter's name for the Orient, or Far East — where spices, silk, porcelain, gems, and precious metals promised large profits.

Chapter 1 → Columbus's Search for the In.text: Turned down in Portugal, the Italian sailor Christopher Columbus carried his plan for a westward route to the Indies to Spain, where King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella agreed to pay. Three ships left in August 1492, and land came into sight on October 12. Convinced he had raised the East Indies, he named the people he met Indians. His hope of spreading Catholicism was pursued the wrong way: he mistreated those people and shipped some to Spain as slaves.

Chapter 1 → Other Spanish Explorers.text: Spain worked the Central and South American coasts first, then pushed inland behind the conquistadors, where the treasure lay. A few looked north instead, winning Spain claims in Florida, Texas, and the Southwest. Juan Ponce de León explored Florida in 1513; Hernando de Soto left Florida in 1539, crossed the Southeast, and came upon the Mississippi; Francisco Coronado rode north from Mexico in 1540 hunting Cíbola's golden cities and was the first European ever to see the Grand Canyon.

Chapter 1 → The French.text: A northern water route to the Far East was what France wanted; what France got was a fur business. Through the 1600s the French settled the St. Lawrence, the Mississippi, and the Great Lakes, using the waterways as roads inland and swapping axes, pots, and clothing for beaver, fox, otter, and moose skins. Forts, missions, and trading posts guarded the traders instead of towns. Samuel de Champlain, the Father of New France, raised the fort that grew into Quebec.

Chapter 1 → Sea Dogs and the Spanish Arm.text: England's claim to the Atlantic coast of North America dates from John Cabot in 1497. Through the 1500s a band of English captains, the Sea Dogs, worked as pirates — wrecking Spanish harbors, seizing treasure ships, and choking off the wealth flowing home to Spain, which is why Spain was so angry. Sir Francis Drake was the most famous. Spain named him the master thief; England cheered him, and Elizabeth I knighted him aboard the Golden Hind.

Chapter 1 → The Lost Colony.text: Two colonizing expeditions to Roanoke Island were organized and paid for by Sir Walter Raleigh, an English nobleman the queen favored — though he never crossed to the New World himself. Famine, Indian attacks, and weak leadership broke the first attempt of 1585, and its settlers sailed home within a year. John White took charge of the second in 1587, went back for supplies, and was held in England three years by the fighting with Spain.

Chapter 1 → Jamestown.text: Jamestown, England's first permanent colony, was built in May 1607 on the James River by men the Virginia Company — London merchants — sent seeking gold, silver, and adventure; the Powhatan, a Woodland people, already held that land. Gentlemen would not work, and farmers quit when whole harvests went to a common storehouse. Smith's no-work-no-food rule and his dealings with the Indians revived it; after the starving time came supplies, a new governor, and tobacco. Burgesses first met in 1619.

Chapter 1 → Pocahontas.text: Daughter of the Powhatan chief, Pocahontas carried food and furs to the colonists, and John Smith credited her with saving his life. The English kidnapped her in 1613 and held her for ransom. In captivity she learned English, became a Christian, and took the name Rebecca. Her marriage to the tobacco planter John Rolfe in 1614 brought a spell of peace. The Rolfes sailed to England in 1616, where she met King James I; illness killed her before her return.

Chapter 1 → Empires in Western Africa.text: Trade in gold, salt, ivory, and slaves made the empires of western Africa enormously rich for centuries. Ghana taxed goods crossing its territory at the Sahara's edge and peaked about AD 1000, then declined as gold turned up elsewhere; Mali absorbed it and took Timbuktu and Gao. Mali's Mansa Musa went on pilgrimage to Mecca early in the 1300s, spending so lavishly on the way that he threw the places he passed, Egypt worst of all, into economic trouble.

Chapter 1 → Africans in America.text: A Dutch ship put about twenty Africans ashore in Virginia in 1619, the year the first large group of women reached Jamestown. They were evidently treated as indentured servants: laborers who worked set years to repay their passage, then went free. That soon changed. Almost every African who followed came as a slave — roughly five times a servant's cost, bound for life, any children counted the master's property. Demand for cheap labor made the market.

Chapter 1 → Esteban.text: A century before Africans landed at Jamestown, Esteban, a Moroccan enslaved by a Spanish nobleman who had turned explorer, was already in the South. His party explored Cuba and Florida, fled pursuit along the Gulf Coast, and wrecked its makeshift boats near Galveston. Natives held the eighty survivors captive; four escaped and wandered the Southwest for years. Sold to Mexico City's governor, Esteban scouted ahead of a friar toward Cíbola, marking his finds with crosses, until natives killed him.

Chapter 1 → The Middle Passage.text: Captured Africans crossed the Atlantic by the route named the Middle Passage: the middle of three stages, after the march to the African coast, before the sale to owners in the Americas. Because profit rose with numbers, ships were loaded until captives lay piled on top of each other or chained in rows, for anywhere from five weeks to four months. Filth, foul air, and disease killed many; the sick were sometimes thrown into the sea.

items.stem: The chapter says the name Olmec means what?
options: Sky people, after the star charts they painted on their temple walls
Rubber people, after the uses they found for the rubber tree
River people, after the wide valleys where they planted maize and cassava
Mound people, after the earthen tombs they raised over their dead

items.stem: Who led the Aztec empire when the Spanish conquistadors overthrew it?
options: Powhatan, who watched the newcomers with deep suspicion
Hernando Cortés, who was pushing inland in search of treasure
Montezuma, under whom the empire was still expanding
Mansa Musa, who spent gold freely wherever he traveled

items.stem: What was Tenochtitlan?
options: The Maya city of step pyramids abandoned by about AD 900
The trading post Ghana built at the edge of the Sahara desert
The mountaintop city the Inca raised in hard-to-reach country
The large city the Aztecs built on drained swampland

items.stem: Mexico City stands today on the site of which earlier city?
options: Tenochtitlan, built by the Aztecs
Cahokia, built by the mound builders
Machu Picchu, built by the Inca
Timbuktu, taken over by the empire of Mali

items.stem: The chapter says the Olmec and the Maya put their study of the sun, moon, and stars together with advances in mathematics. What did they create with it?
options: A 365-day calendar
A system of irrigation that carried water out to the planted fields
A network of paved roads that tied their distant cities together
A written language whose symbols resembled Egyptian hieroglyphics

items.stem: The chapter has a name for the Spanish soldiers who took the Aztec and Incan empires by force. Which name is it?
options: Sea Dogs
Indentured servants
Conquistadors
Mound builders

items.stem: The Aztecs had great numbers of people and were skilled at fighting. How does the chapter explain the fall of their empire to the Spanish?
options: Their neighbors rose against Montezuma and handed the city over to the Spanish soldiers
Their warriors had marched south to fight the Inca and were not at home to defend it
Their numbers were no match for Spanish weapons, and disease cut them roughly in half
Their capital had been emptied by a long famine before the Spanish soldiers ever arrived

items.stem: True or false: the chapter dates the Olmec civilization centuries earlier than the Aztec civilization.
options: True
False
justify_options: The chapter dates the Olmec decline to about 400 BC and the founding of the Aztec empire to the AD 1200s
The chapter says the Olmec carved their stone heads only after the Aztecs had drained the swampland for Tenochtitlan
The chapter says the Olmec and the Aztecs shared the same cities and rose together in the rainforests of Guatemala

items.stem: Put these three peoples in the order the chapter says they rose.
options: The Olmec, who farmed southern Mexico centuries before Christ
The Maya, whose golden age of cities and step pyramids began about AD 250
The Aztecs, whose warrior empire was founded in the AD 1200s

items.stem: What does the chapter mean when it calls a group nomadic?
options: They settled beside a river and raised crops in one place
They obeyed a single chief who ruled several tribes at once
They traded with other tribes for the food they could not grow
They moved constantly in search of game and wild plants

items.stem: Southwestern tribes made houses out of adobe. What is adobe, according to the chapter?
options: Blocks cut out of snow and hard ice
Logs stacked and packed with earth
A dried mixture of clay and straw
Cedar planks split from very tall trees

items.stem: Which tribes does the chapter call cliff dwellers, and what did they build?
options: Great Plains tribes, who set up cone-shaped tepees beside rivers and lakes
Southeastern tribes, who piled up earthen mounds for tombs and ceremonies
Northwestern tribes, who raised cedar houses along the ocean and rivers
Southwestern tribes, who cut elaborate houses into the sides of cliffs

items.stem: What were the mounds of the mound builders used for, and where did those people live?
options: Storing grain and sheltering families, in the forests of the Northeast
Tombs and religious ceremonies, in the dry country of the far Southwest
Tombs and religious ceremonies, in the Ohio Valley and the Southeast
Watching for enemies and signaling, on the plains beyond the Mississippi

items.stem: Define animism as the chapter uses the word.
options: The belief that all natural objects, living or not, have souls
The belief that the spirits of dead chiefs come back as animals
The belief that one Great Spirit made the world and then withdrew
The belief that the gods require blood before they will send rain

items.stem: The Inuit burned one thing for light in the far north. What was it?
options: Pine pitch, gathered from the forests to the south
Whale oil, taken from the animals they hunted
Driftwood, collected along the edge of the sea ice
Buffalo tallow, carried up from the Great Plains

items.stem: True or false: the chapter says Southwestern tribes had to keep moving because the dry country could not feed them.
options: True
False
justify_options: They farmed the desert, gathered wild plants, and hunted small animals, and they built houses to stay in
They followed the bison herds across the grasslands and carried their homes with them from camp to camp
They lived on wild nuts and berries because the land between the two mountain ranges could not be farmed at all

items.stem: The chapter explains why some tribes built permanent villages while others kept moving. What made the difference?
options: Whether the tribe had horses to carry its goods from camp to camp
Whether they had learned to build with stone instead of wood
Whether their food supply stayed steady in one place
Whether their chief was strong enough to hold them together

items.stem: Which explorer does the chapter call the best known Viking adventurer, believed to have reached North America about AD 1000?
options: Leif Ericson, who sailed west from Greenland
John Cabot, who claimed the Atlantic coast for England
Jacques Cartier, who sailed up a great northern river
Amerigo Vespucci, who explored the coasts to the south

items.stem: Leif Ericson found land in what is now Newfoundland, Canada. What did he name it?
options: New France
San Salvador
Greenland
Vinland

items.stem: Much of the early exploration was a search for new routes to the Indies. What did Europeans want from there?
options: Spices, silk, porcelain, gems, and precious metals
Gold from the mines of Mexico and silver out of Peru
Horses, cattle, wheat seed, and iron tools for farms
Furs, timber, dried fish, and whale oil for lamps

items.stem: Columbus needed someone to pay for his voyage west. Who finally agreed?

King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain
King Philip II, who ruled Spain a century later

On the islands of the Caribbean and the coasts of South America
Along the coast of Virginia and up the James River from Chesapeake Bay
Along the St. Lawrence and Mississippi and around the Great Lakes

items.stem: Why were merchants and monarchs willing to pay for voyages in search of new trade routes?
options: Their ships were sitting idle in harbor and needed the work
They wanted to prove to the doubters that the earth is round
They hoped to plant settlers who would send back raw materials
Great profits could be made by bringing Eastern goods home

items.stem: Why did the French build forts, missions, and trading posts instead of well-organized towns?
options: The king refused to allow any settlement more than a mile inland
They expected to leave as soon as the water route east was found
They stood at key places to guard French traders and trappers
The Huguenots who arrived first would not live in crowded towns

items.stem: Who were the Sea Dogs?
options: Portuguese sailors who first fitted caravels with new sails
Spanish captains who guarded the treasure fleets homeward
English sea captains who raided Spanish ports and ships
French trappers who carried furs down to the trading posts

options: Jacques Cartier
Sir Francis Drake

items.stem: Why did the Sea Dogs anger Spain so much?
options: They carried Protestant preachers into Spanish harbors
They sold English weapons to the Indians of the Caribbean
They planted English colonies on land the Spanish had claimed
They cut off the flow of riches from the Americas to Spain

items.stem: The English and the Spanish saw Sir Francis Drake very differently. How does the chapter describe the difference?
options: Spain called him a rival; England thought him a harmless fool
Spain called him a thief; England made him a popular hero
Spain feared his guns; England feared he would change sides
Spain wanted him hanged; England wanted him to stay ashore

items.stem: What was Jamestown, and when was it founded?
options: The first representative assembly in America, created in 1619
The first Spanish city in North America to last, founded in 1565
The first permanent English settlement in North America, 1607
The first English settlement in North America, which vanished, 1587

items.stem: Who sent the colonists who founded Jamestown?
options: Sir Walter Raleigh, who had already tried at Roanoke
King James I, who sent his own navy across with them
The Church of England, which wanted an Indian mission
The Virginia Company, a group of London merchants

items.stem: What were the Jamestown colonists and the company behind them hoping to gain?
options: Freedom to worship as they believed God's Word teaches
A northern water route through the continent to the Far East
Gold and silver, adventure, and a profit for the investors
Furs to trade with the Indians up and down the rivers

items.stem: Who declared that any man who did not work would not eat?
options: John Smith, a rough soldier who demanded obedience
John Rolfe, the planter who married Pocahontas
Powhatan, the chief the colonists dealt with warily
Lord De La Warr, the governor who arrived in 1610

items.stem: Besides making the colonists work, what else does the chapter credit John Smith with doing?
options: Bringing the first shipload of women over to the settlement
Starting a relationship with the Indians for food and advice
Carrying the first tobacco seed across the ocean to Virginia
Setting up the House of Burgesses to pass laws for the colony

items.stem: Which Indians lived in the part of Virginia where the English decided to settle?

The Croatoan, who lived near Roanoke Island
The Powhatan, a group of Woodland Indians
The Cherokee, who lived in the Southeast region

items.stem: Which crop became a profitable cash crop for Jamestown?
options: Maize, which the Woodland Indians had planted
Cassava, a root vegetable the Olmec grew in Mexico
Tobacco, which the colonists sold for a profit
Squash, which grew well in the Virginia soil

items.stem: Whom did Pocahontas marry, and what followed the marriage?
options: John Smith, the soldier; the colonists went back to work
John Cabot, the explorer; England claimed the coast after it
John White, the Roanoke leader; the colony then vanished
John Rolfe, a tobacco planter; a period of peace followed

items.stem: What happened to Pocahontas in 1613, and whom did she later meet in England?
options: The English kidnapped her; she later met King James I
She was sent to school in London; she met the Virginia Company
Her father sent her as a peace offering; she met King Philip II
The English hired her as a guide; she met Queen Elizabeth I

items.stem: Who organized the two colonizing expeditions to Roanoke Island?
options: Sir Francis Drake, the queen's favorite pirate
John White, who was left in charge in 1587
Sir Walter Raleigh, an English nobleman
The Virginia Company, a group of London merchants

items.stem: What was the Virginia House of Burgesses?
options: The first representative assembly in America
The company of London merchants that sent the settlers
The first English church built in the Americas
The council of chiefs who spoke for the Powhatan tribes

items.stem: What problem was John Smith's work-or-eat rule meant to fix?
options: Men had used up all the gunpowder hunting for game
Men had stopped working, and food had run short
Men had begun trading their tools away to the Indians
Men were deserting the fort to live in Indian villages

items.stem: Why does the chapter say Jamestown played a role in the beginning of the American republic?
options: Its colonists chose burgesses who met to pass laws
Its settlers were the first English to cross the ocean
Its governor was the first man ever appointed by a king
Its charter was written before any other colony's charter

items.stem: After the starving time, what does the chapter say steadied the colony?
options: Supplies and a new governor, crops that fed it, and tobacco
A shipment of gold and silver found upriver from the fort
A treaty with Powhatan that ended every quarrel for good
The arrival of Sir Walter Raleigh with a hundred more settlers

items.stem: True or false: Sir Walter Raleigh sailed to Roanoke Island himself and led the colony there.
options: True
False
justify_options: The chapter says he never journeyed to the New World; he organized and paid for the two attempts
The chapter says he led the first attempt of 1585 himself and then handed the second one over to John White
The chapter says he stayed away three years because the fighting with Spain kept his ships in England

items.stem: What does the chapter say about the roughly twenty Africans a Dutch ship landed in Virginia in 1619?
options: They were sold as slaves the day the ship reached Virginia
They were carried on to the Caribbean a few weeks later
They were free sailors who chose to stay in the colony
They appear to have been treated as indentured servants

items.stem: What was an indentured servant, as the chapter explains the term?
options: Someone who was paid wages by the Virginia Company
Someone who worked a few years to pay for the crossing
Someone who worked for a master for the whole of his life
Someone who owned land and rented it out to other farmers

items.stem: Which empire did Mansa Musa rule, and where did he travel in the early 1300s?
options: Songhai, and he sailed south with the Portuguese
Ghana, and he crossed the Sahara to trade for salt
Mali, and he made a pilgrimage to Mecca
Timbuktu, and he traveled to the coast to meet traders

items.stem: What does the chapter say created a market for slaves from West Africa?
options: The tribal wars fought along the western coast of Africa
European and American demand for cheap labor
The Portuguese need for sailors aboard their ships
A shortage of gold in the empire of Songhai

items.stem: Who is considered the first African in America?
options: Esteban, a Moroccan slave of a Spanish explorer
Mansa Musa, the ruler of the empire of Mali
Zheng He, an admiral of the Ming dynasty
One of the twenty Africans landed in Virginia in 1619

items.stem: What happened to Esteban's party after their makeshift boats capsized near Galveston?
options: Natives held them captive until only four were left
A Spanish ship picked them up again within a few weeks
They founded a small settlement and stayed on that coast
They walked back to Cuba along the coast within a year

items.stem: How does the chapter contrast a slave with an indentured servant?
options: A slave cost about the same but could buy his freedom back
A slave was paid wages while a servant worked for nothing
A slave worked in the fields while a servant worked indoors
A slave cost about five times as much and served for life

items.stem: How did Mansa Musa's wealth affect other civilizations?
options: His spending on the way to Mecca upset economies, Egypt's worst
His armies took Timbuktu and Gao away from the rulers of Songhai
His gold paid for the Portuguese caravels that first sailed to India
His pilgrimage opened a new trade route between Mali and the Indies

items.stem: The chapter says the transatlantic slave trade exploded when Europeans arrived. How does it explain that?
options: Barbary pirates seized whole villages and sold them in the Americas
Buyers wanted cheap labor, so Africans raided to meet the demand
The Portuguese made slaveholding a condition of every trade deal
African rulers ran out of gold and sold captives to replace it

items.stem: The chapter says it is uncertain how the first people reached the Americas. What is one possible route it gives?
options: A crossing from the coast of western Africa
A land bridge that linked Asia to Alaska
A voyage with the Viking ships about AD 1000
A chain of islands running down from Iceland

items.stem: Where does the chapter's account of people spreading over the earth begin?
options: With the call of Abraham to go to a new land
With the flood of Noah and the ark on Ararat
With the exodus of Israel out of the land of Egypt
With the confusing of languages at Babel

items.stem: How does the chapter say the native peoples showed the capabilities God gives every image-bearer?
options: They gathered into one nation under a single powerful chief
They set aside forests where nobody was allowed to hunt at all
They kept careful written records of everything their tribes had done
They shaped their environments skillfully and built lasting works

items.stem: What was the Middle Passage?
options: The sale of captives to slave owners in the Americas
The march that carried captives to the coast of Africa
The ocean crossing that carried captives to the Americas
The overland route that carried salt south across the Sahara

items.stem: Why does the chapter say 'perhaps' about the land bridge instead of stating it as settled fact?
options: It says how and when the first people arrived is uncertain
It says the Bible names the exact route the first people traveled
It says only the Vikings ever crossed from one side to the other
It says the land bridge melted before anyone could cross over it

items.stem: Europeans often called the native peoples backward or savage. What does the chapter say they were failing to see?
options: The number of warriors each tribe could put into the field
The treaties the tribes had already signed with the Spanish
The wealth in gold and silver that the tribes had gathered up
The abilities God gives to everyone who bears His image

items.stem: True or false: the chapter says slave traders packed as many people as they could onto a ship in order to make as much money as possible.
options: True
False
justify_options: People lay stacked on one another or chained side by side with no room to move
Ships carried few captives at a time so that the healthy ones would fetch a higher price
Traders fed the captives rice, cornmeal, or yams twice a day to keep them strong enough

question_sets.label: Explorers and what each one did

shared_options.theme: a hunt for the golden cities of Cíbola that ended in the Southwest
shared_options.correction: the Spaniard who rode north from Mexico in 1540 after Cíbola's golden cities, found the adobe villages of the Pueblo instead, and was the first European to see the Grand Canyon

shared_options.theme: a march through the Southeast that ended at a great river
shared_options.correction: the conquistador who started from Florida in 1539 hoping for riches in Indian settlements and traveled the Southeast until he came upon the Mississippi River

shared_options.theme: the first Spanish exploration of Florida
shared_options.correction: the first Spaniard to explore Florida, arriving in 1513 in search of riches, and possibly the first European to see land that is now the United States

shared_options.theme: French exploration of the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes
shared_options.correction: the French explorer called the Father of New France, who explored the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes region and built the fort that became the city of Quebec

shared_options.theme: English raids on Spanish ports and a voyage on around the world
shared_options.correction: the most famous Sea Dog, who plundered Spanish ports, escaped by sailing on around South America and across the Pacific, and was knighted aboard the Golden Hind

shared_options.theme: paying for English colonies without ever sailing to them
shared_options.correction: the English nobleman who organized and financed the two Roanoke expeditions of 1585 and 1587 but never journeyed to the New World himself

questions.focus: a search for the legendary golden cities of Cíbola
questions.stem: In 1540 this explorer came north from Mexico hunting the legendary golden cities of Cíbola. He never found them, but he did find the adobe villages of the Pueblo Indians, and he was the first European to see the Grand Canyon. Who was he?

questions.focus: an inland march through the Southeast that ended at a great river
questions.stem: Hoping to find riches in the Indian settlements of North America, this Spaniard started out from Florida in 1539 and traveled through the Southeast until he came upon the Mississippi River. Who was he?

questions.focus: the first Spanish exploration of Florida
questions.stem: This Spaniard arrived in 1513, searching for riches among other things, and was the first of his countrymen to explore Florida. The chapter adds that he may have been the first European to see land that is now the United States. Who was he?

questions.focus: French exploration of the St. Lawrence, and a fort that grew into a city
questions.stem: This explorer has been called the Father of New France. He further explored the St. Lawrence River and the Great Lakes region, and he built the fort that later became the city of Quebec. Who was he?

questions.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Sea Dogs and the Spanish Armada
questions.focus: raiding Spanish ports and then sailing on around the world to escape
questions.stem: In 1577 this English captain sailed down the coast of South America, plundering Spanish ports and capturing treasure ships. To escape the Spanish patrols he kept going — around South America, across the Pacific, and around Africa's Cape of Good Hope — and came home to a triumphant welcome. Who was he?

questions.focus: paying for two colonies without ever crossing the ocean
questions.stem: This English nobleman, another favorite of the queen, organized two colonizing expeditions to Roanoke Island — one in 1585 and another in 1587 — although he never journeyed to the New World himself. Who was he?

shared_options.theme: pushing inland after treasure and planting a church wherever land was claimed
shared_options.correction: the Europeans whose conquistadors pushed inland after treasure, who began colonizing Mexico as early as 1519, and who established their language, customs, and Roman Catholic religion in the lands they claimed

shared_options.theme: fur trading from forts and posts along the rivers and lakes
shared_options.correction: the Europeans who settled the St. Lawrence and Mississippi and the Great Lakes, traded tools and clothing for furs, and built forts, missions, and trading posts instead of organized towns

shared_options.theme: an early claim to the Atlantic coast, and captains who preyed on Spanish shipping
shared_options.correction: the Europeans whose claim to the Atlantic coast dates from John Cabot in 1497 and whose Sea Dogs raided Spanish harbors and treasure ships through the 1500s

shared_options.theme: the ship design and the voyages that made long-distance exploration possible
shared_options.correction: the Europeans who adapted small fishing boats into the fast ships called caravels, sailed down and around Africa toward India, and later joined the trade of the Songhai empire

shared_options.theme: northern seamen who reached America centuries before Columbus
shared_options.correction: the Norsemen of northern Europe, who planted colonies in Iceland and Greenland and reached Newfoundland about AD 1000, though the rest of Europe never heard of the voyages

questions.focus: conquistadors hunting treasure inland, and a language and a church planted in the claimed lands
questions.stem: Their conquistadors pushed inland from the coasts hunting treasure, they began to colonize Mexico as early as 1519, and wherever they claimed land they established their language, their customs, and their Roman Catholic religion. Which Europeans does the chapter describe?

questions.focus: using the rivers and lakes as roads into the interior for the fur trade
questions.stem: They settled along the St. Lawrence and Mississippi Rivers and around the Great Lakes, using the water as roads into the interior. They traded axes, pots, and clothing to the Indians for the skins of beavers, foxes, otters, and moose, and they built forts and trading posts rather than towns. Which Europeans does the chapter describe?

questions.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → Sea Dogs and the Spanish Armada
questions.focus: an early claim to the Atlantic coast, followed by captains who raided Spanish shipping
questions.stem: As early as 1497 one of their explorers laid claim to the Atlantic coast of North America, and through the 1500s their sea captains raided Spanish harbors and seized treasure ships. Which Europeans does the chapter describe?

questions.focus: the ship design that let Europeans sail far from shore
questions.stem: Before the 1400s few Europeans went far out to sea, because their ships could not handle rough conditions away from the shore. These people solved that by adapting small fishing boats for long-distance travel with specially designed sails, producing the fast ships called caravels. Which Europeans does the chapter describe?

questions.focus: reaching North America about AD 1000, unknown to the rest of Europe
questions.stem: Seamen out of northern Europe, they planted colonies in Iceland and Greenland and then sailed west to Canada about AD 1000. The rest of Europe never learned of those voyages. Which Europeans does the chapter describe?

question_sets.label: Indian regions and the tribes that lived in them
question_sets.source_anchor: Chapter 1 → The People of North America

shared_options.theme: desert farming and homes made of cliff rock, dried clay, and logs
shared_options.correction: the region of the Pueblo, Apache, Hopi, and Navajo, whose people farmed the desert, gathered wild plants, hunted small animals, and built cliff houses, adobe homes, and hogans

shared_options.theme: mounds of earth raised for tombs and religious ceremonies
shared_options.correction: the region of the mound builders and of the Cherokee, Seminole, and Creek, where earthen mounds served as tombs and ceremonial sites and Cahokia held more people in 1200 than London did

shared_options.theme: making everything a family needs out of what the frozen north supplies
shared_options.correction: the region near the Arctic Circle where the Inuit shaped igloos from snow and ice and hunted caribou, whales, seals, and walruses for food, clothing, light, and boat skins

shared_options.theme: forest tribes whose steady crops let them build permanent villages
shared_options.correction: the region from the Atlantic to the Mississippi where the Algonquian, Huron, Iroquois, and Powhatan hunted, fished, and planted maize, squash, and tobacco, living in wigwams and longhouses

questions.focus: the tribes of the dry country and the three ways they fed themselves
questions.stem: The Pueblo, the Apache, the Hopi, and the Navajo lived here. They farmed the desert, gathered wild plants, and hunted small animals, and the region is known for turquoise jewelry, pottery, and woven goods. Which region does the chapter describe?

questions.focus: the tribes of the region where earthen mounds were raised
questions.stem: The Cherokee, the Seminole, and the Creek lived here, in the same part of the country as the people who raised mounds of earth for tombs and religious ceremonies. Which region does the chapter describe?

questions.focus: hunting the animals of the frozen north for everything a family needed
questions.stem: The people here hunted caribou, whales, seals, and walruses for food and clothing. They burned whale oil for light and stretched the skins of hunted animals over their small boats and kayaks. Which region does the chapter describe?

questions.focus: the region the Powhatan of Virginia belonged to
questions.stem: The Powhatan lived in villages along the rivers of Virginia, where they fished, hunted, and farmed, and where the English later built Jamestown. The chapter groups them with the tribes of one of its seven regions. Which region is it?
